title: Monolith vs. Orchestrator Cost Simulator
paper: 2609.05758v2 - Dynamic Response
pitch: Single-page toy: a slider set (conversation complexity, escalation rate, tool count) drives two animated pipelines side-by-side -- one giant monolithic LLM call, one bounded ReAct orchestrator with typed tools -- showing live latency, hallucination-rate, and $-per-1k-turns diverge in real time, seeded from the paper's actual numbers (8.3%->89.1% selector precision, 2.14%->0% hallucination, 3.87s->2.24s latency, 10x cost cut).
discussion_why: mild surprise value ("wait, smaller+structured beats bigger") but limited betting/poker/games hook

title: Bet-Slip Orchestrator: typed-tool agent for sportsbook support
paper: 2609.05758v2 - Dynamic Response
pitch: Apply the paper's architecture (bounded ReAct orchestrator + typed entity/action tools + small generator) to a sportsbook customer-support use case -- e.g., "cash out my bet slip", "why was my parlay voided" -- to kill structured-action hallucination on money-moving actions, which is exactly the failure mode that's catastrophic in a betting product.
discussion_why: betting-relevant: a hallucinated cash-out action is a real financial-safety story people will argue about

title: Why Bigger LLM Isn't Better: the customer-support case study
paper: 2609.05758v2 - Dynamic Response
pitch: Explainer video walking through how a huge company swapped one giant model for a modular agent swarm and got more accurate, faster, and 10x cheaper -- a concrete rebuttal to "just use the biggest model" hype, framed around the specific before/after metrics.
discussion_why: solid AI-engineering discourse fodder but not natively a betting/poker/games conversation

title: AgentOps Audit: monolith-to-orchestrator migration service
paper: 2609.05758v2 - Dynamic Response
pitch: Small consultancy/product that audits a company's single-prompt LLM support bot, replays their real transcripts through a typed-tool orchestrator prototype, and hands back a report projecting the hallucination/cost/latency deltas -- selling the exact before/after framing this paper validates.
discussion_why: niche B2B pitch, low shareability outside AI-ops circles

title: GameFilm-QL: relational query engine over NBA broadcast footage
paper: 2609.05756v1 - Concord
pitch: Port Concord's Video Relational Algebra idea (transcript-first + detect-track-join instead of raw-frame MLLM calls) onto NBA/NFL broadcast footage for SharpLab/nba-modeling: query things like "every clip where a driving lane opened after a screen" by joining tracked player positions instead of feeding hours of video to a multimodal model, cutting analysis cost the same way the paper cut it to ~5% of video duration sent to the MLLM.
discussion_why: directly feeds NBA-props edge-finding, the kind of "free alpha" tooling a betting Discord will actually want to poke holes in

title: Video-Query Cost Calculator
paper: 2609.05756v1 - Concord
pitch: Single HTML page: pick a query type (narrated-video transcript search vs. cross-camera object join) and drag a "footage hours" slider; it animates what fraction of the raw video Concord-style optimization actually needs to send to a costly multimodal model, live-computing dollars saved using the paper's real numbers (87% cost reduction, F1 .364->.813 with zero MLLM calls on the tracking task).
discussion_why: the "wait, you can skip the AI entirely and still win" twist (F1 .364->.813 with zero MLLM calls) is a fun surprise beat

title: GameFilm SQL: cheap video-querying SaaS for scouting/betting shops
paper: 2609.05756v1 - Concord
pitch: Package the transcript-first / detect-track-join optimization as an API that lets sportsbooks, scouting departments, and prop shops run natural-language queries over game film for a fraction of the cost of brute-force MLLM video analysis -- pitch is literally "query a whole season for what one game used to cost."
discussion_why: sits right at the sports+betting+decision-theory intersection people on a SharpLab-style server care about

title: How to Make AI Watch an Entire NBA Season for $10
paper: 2609.05756v1 - Concord
pitch: Explainer/demo video building a toy version of the video relational algebra on public game clips, showing the cost collapse from "feed every frame to GPT" to "transcript+tracking then join" -- a viral-shaped "AI cost hack" narrative.
discussion_why: sports-video-for-cheap has obvious pull for anyone doing prop research or scouting on a budget

title: The Challenger Disaster and the AI Labs Repeating It
paper: 2609.05749v1 - Normalization of Deviance
pitch: Video essay mapping Challenger, Three Mile Island, and the 737 MAX onto contemporary AI lab practices, built around the paper's core, unsettling claim: orgs can follow every safety process to the letter and still walk straight into catastrophe -- ending on "the pre-disaster period is still interruptible, if anyone's watching for it."
discussion_why: prime debate bait -- "which AI lab is currently in its Challenger phase" is the kind of question that splits a room

title: Normalization of Deviance: the slippery-slope game
paper: 2609.05749v1 - Normalization of Deviance
pitch: Single-file choose-your-own-adventure HTML game: you're an org manager (AI lab, refinery, or NASA program, player's choice) making a string of small, individually-reasonable safety trade-offs under deadline pressure; a hidden risk meter creeps up invisibly each round, and the game reveals -- after the inevitable disaster -- exactly which "reasonable" decisions compounded, letting players replay and see how early they could've caught it.
discussion_why: the "wait, I made every individually defensible call and still caused a disaster" gut-punch is exactly the kind of thing a decision-theory-minded Discord will replay and argue about

title: Deviance Scorecard: org self-assessment tool
paper: 2609.05749v1 - Normalization of Deviance
pitch: A short interactive checklist site that scores a team/company against the paper's normalization-of-deviance red flags (compliance-without-substance, silenced dissent, incremental risk creep, deadline-driven waivers) and returns a "how close to Challenger are you" risk profile.
discussion_why: useful but more of a corporate self-help tool than a spark for banter

title: LLM Calibration Casino
paper: 2609.01182v1 - LLMPEDIA
pitch: A single-file slot-machine-styled page: it shows a real-sounding factual claim generated by an LLM, you place a chip bet on TRUE or FALSE before revealing the verdict, and your running bankroll gets crushed by the house edge baked into the paper's real base rate -- LLM claims are only 68.4% factual (21pp below what MMLU implies) with ~31% unverifiable "insufficient" claims acting as house-edge landmines.
discussion_why: literally a betting mechanic wrapped around an AI-trust surprise stat -- maximal overlap with gambling + decision-theory + "wait, really?"

title: Multi-Model Belief Comparator
paper: 2609.01182v1 - LLMPEDIA

discussion_why: the cross-model disagreement angle ("which model is more full of it") is inherently arguable

title: I Fact-Checked 1.3 Million Things ChatGPT Believes
paper: 2609.01182v1 - LLMPEDIA
pitch: Explainer/quiz-format video walking through the LLMPEDIA audit methodology and results, pausing periodically to quiz the viewer "true, false, or unverifiable?" on real extracted claims before revealing the 68.4% factuality rate.
discussion_why: quiz format plus a genuinely shocking headline number drives strong "wait, really?" reactions

title: Confidence vs. Correctness Scatter
paper: 2609.01182v1 - LLMPEDIA
pitch: Interactive scatter plot (built from the paper's published breakdowns) letting you filter by model, topic, and political-persona variant to see where LLM confidence diverges most from verified accuracy -- a self-contained data-viz toy rather than a game.

title: BPE vs. Learned Tokenizer, Side by Side

discussion_why: genuinely satisfying nerd-toy but has no natural betting/games/gambling hook

title: Tokenization Is the Hidden Bottleneck for Small AI Models
paper: 2609.01151v1 - Subword Segmental BabyLMs

discussion_why: solid ML-education content but a niche audience outside tokenizer nerds

title: Open Subword-Segmental Tokenizer Trainer
paper: 2609.01151v1 - Subword Segmental BabyLMs
pitch: Small open-source library implementing the paper's learnable segmentation approach so other BabyLM-challenge entrants (or anyone training a tiny model) can swap in a jointly-learned tokenizer instead of fixed BPE.

title: Optical Compression Slider
paper: 2609.01147 - On the Design Fundamentals of Pixel Text Representation Learning
pitch: Single HTML page: paste text, it renders as a pixel image (canvas), then a slider progressively downsamples/JPEG-compresses the rendered image while a mocked-up 'semantic retention' curve (calibrated to the paper's reported 80%-token-compression robustness) shows how much meaning survives before the text becomes visually unreadable. Makes the counterintuitive 'you can read text as a blurry picture and still retrieve it' claim tangible.
discussion_why: wins on surprise -- 'wait, you can shrink text images by 80% and an AI still reads them?'

title: Why Some AIs Read Words as Pictures
paper: 2609.01147 - On the Design Fundamentals of Pixel Text Representation Learning
pitch: Explainer on the pixel-language-model trend (PIXEL, CLIPPO, Pixel Linguist II): why ditching tokenizers and rendering text as images fixes multilingual/OOV problems and enables 'optical context compression' -- screenshotting a doc instead of tokenizing it to save context budget.
discussion_why: wins on surprise for an AI-curious audience unfamiliar with tokenizer-free models

title: PixelDoc: Screenshot-Based Context Compression
paper: 2609.01147 - On the Design Fundamentals of Pixel Text Representation Learning
pitch: Wrap the open-sourced Pixel Linguist II encoder in a small RAG pipeline that stores long documents as rendered pixel-image chunks instead of tokenized text, cutting context-window/token costs for retrieval while staying robust under heavy compression -- a real efficiency play for long-doc chat tools.
discussion_why: wins on relatability for anyone burning tokens on long-context RAG

title: Judge Showdown: Holistic vs. Decomposed
paper: 2609.01139 - Does task decomposition improve automatic NLG evaluation?

discussion_why: wins on debate -- mirrors the poker/sports argument of 'granular breakdown' handicappers vs. 'gut number' bettors, and which actually wins

title: LLM-as-Judge Folk Wisdom, Debunked
paper: 2609.01139 - Does task decomposition improve automatic NLG evaluation?

discussion_why: wins on surprise for anyone who has built an LLM grading rubric assuming decomposition helps

title: Dual-Mode Grader Harness

discussion_why: wins on relatability for anyone building internal AI QA tooling

discussion_why: wins on fit -- directly recreates the 'wisdom of crowds vs. upset noise' argument every sports/poker Discord has, with actual math backing it

title: Consensus Power Rankings via SVD
paper: 2609.01135 - Overfitting Mitigation via Singular Value Decomposition in Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding
pitch: Feed SharpLab's collected handicapper picks / power rankings / model outputs into a pairwise-comparison matrix and apply the paper's low-rank SVD denoising to extract a 'true consensus' ranking that's robust to any single overfit source -- a direct transplant of MBR's utility-matrix trick onto sports betting model aggregation.
discussion_why: wins on fit with betting/sports quant work already underway

title: The Hidden Math Behind Wisdom of Crowds
paper: 2609.01135 - Overfitting Mitigation via Singular Value Decomposition in Minimum Bayes Risk Decoding
pitch: Explainer connecting SVD-MBR's denoising trick to everyday ranking problems -- sports power rankings, poker player pools, ensemble betting model aggregation -- showing visually how a rank-k SVD strips 'noise' (upsets, small-sample flukes) from 'signal' (real skill).
discussion_why: wins on surprise -- a text-generation paper's math turns out to be a generic sports-ranking denoiser

title: AI That Reasons Without Using Words

discussion_why: wins on surprise for anyone who assumes 'more chain-of-thought text = more reasoning'

title: Latent Reasoner for Countdown/Puzzle Games
